trivia_fact: The first recognizable datacenter is arguably the ENIAC room at the University of Pennsylvania (1945). ENIAC occupied 1,800 square feet, weighed 30 tons, and consumed 150 kilowatts — roughly what a small datacenter uses today for a single row of racks.

Hot/cold aisle containment works because server fans pull cool air from the front and exhaust hot air from the back. By alternating rack orientations, you create dedicated cold supply aisles and hot exhaust aisles, preventing hot air from recirculating into server intakes.

The standard 42U server rack height was established by the EIA (Electronic Industries Alliance). One rack unit (1U) equals 1.75 inches (44.45mm), making a 42U rack about 73.5 inches of usable space — tall enough to be practical but short enough for humans to reach the top.

PDU stands for Power Distribution Unit. Datacenter PDUs evolved from simple power strips into intelligent devices that monitor per-outlet power draw, support remote switching, and can alert on overloads — essentially smart power strips on steroids.

Datacenters originally used raised floors (typically 24 inches high) to route the massive cabling required by mainframes. The space was later repurposed for cool air delivery from CRAC units. Modern datacenters increasingly use overhead cabling and in-row cooling instead.

The Uptime Institute Tier Classification system (I-IV) defines datacenter reliability levels. Tier I has no redundancy (99.671% uptime), while Tier IV is fully fault-tolerant with 2N+1 redundancy (99.995% uptime — about 26 minutes downtime per year).

Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) was created by The Green Grid in 2006. It divides total facility power by IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes to computing; the industry average is about 1.58. Google's best facilities achieve 1.10.

Google's datacenter in Hamina, Finland uses cold sea water from the Gulf of Finland for cooling. The facility is built in an old paper mill and pumps filtered sea water through a heat exchange system, eliminating the need for mechanical chillers.

Facebook launched the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011, open-sourcing their datacenter and server designs. This was radical — datacenter hardware had always been proprietary. OCP now includes designs for racks, switches, storage, and even entire buildings.

Microsoft's Project Natick deployed a sealed datacenter on the Scottish seabed in 2018. The underwater pod had a failure rate one-eighth of an equivalent land datacenter, likely because the sealed nitrogen atmosphere eliminated humidity and human-caused damage.

A "lights out" datacenter operates with no on-site staff. Everything is managed remotely, and the lights are literally off to save energy. The concept requires extreme automation, out-of-band management, and robotic maintenance — few facilities achieve it fully.

Many major datacenters cluster in Northern Virginia (Ashburn) because MAE-East, one of the first internet exchange points, was located there. Today, Ashburn handles roughly 70% of global internet traffic and hosts the densest concentration of datacenters on Earth.

Datacenters maintain humidity between 40-60% relative humidity. Too dry and static electricity can damage components; too humid and condensation forms. ASHRAE expanded the acceptable range in 2011, saving significant energy on humidification.

Most datacenters keep 24-72 hours of diesel fuel on-site for backup generators. When utility power fails, UPS batteries bridge the 10-15 second gap while generators start. Some hyperscale datacenters use natural gas turbines instead for cleaner backup power.

Empty rack spaces without blanking panels create a short circuit in the cooling system — hot exhaust air recirculates through the gap back to server intakes. Installing simple plastic blanking panels can reduce cooling costs by 10-20% at near-zero cost.
